the climate has on us. 
It is the start of a reporting journey, though is part of  
a larger journey that the Bank is on both to reduce our 
environmental footprint and to build the capability  
to manage the challenges that a changing climate  
will present to our strategy and business model.

FROM OUR CEO & CHAIR
3
Introduction
The Co-operative is on a journey 
to reduce our environmental 
footprint and to build the capability 
to manage the challenges that 
a changing climate will present 
to our strategy and business 
model. This Climate Report, over 
time, will provide transparent 
and comparable disclosures 
relating to climate-related risks 
and opportunities intended to 
contribute to the shift towards a 
low-emissions, climate-resilient 
future. It will enable the effects 
of climate change to be routinely 
considered in our strategy, decision 
making and capital allocation. 
While opportunities may arise as 
the economy transitions to a low 
carbon world, such as green funding 
initiatives and the potential to attract 
and retain customers by not funding 
carbon-intensive industries, the 
reality is that opportunities will be 
dwarfed by climate risks.
Our initial Climate Report primarily 
focuses on our mortgage portfolio. 
Given the physical risk posed to 
residential property from sea-level 
rise and severe weather events, it 
is a major climate risk to The Co-
operative’s business model. 
Our own climate journey started 
with a group of passionate 
employees who wanted to make 
a positive change to the way that 
The Co-operative operated. The 
initial focus was reduction in waste 
to landfill. This quickly evolved 
into measuring the organisation’s 
carbon footprint and from 
FY21, offsetting our operational 
emissions. In FY23 we joined the 
Toitū Carbonzero programme 
and achieved net carbonzero 
certification. We have commenced 
the process of driving meaningful 
reductions in our emissions.
We have made significant 
progress with scope 1 and 2 
emissions reductions this year. 
However, the bulk of our emissions 
sit in scope 3 and reductions here 
will require engagement with our 
suppliers and driving behavioural 
change across our value chain. 
We are also yet to begin the 
process of formally measuring 
our financed emissions.
Next year’s report will provide 
quantitative detail for the projected 
impact on The Co-operative of 
the scenarios that we outline 
in this document, further 
development of our emission 
reduction targets particularly 
around scope 3 emissions, the 
ongoing development of our risk 
management framework and 
quantification of financial impacts 
of climate risks and opportunities.
Thank you for taking the time to 
read our initial Climate Report 
and we look forward to updating 
you with further progress in future 
reports.

STATEMENT OF COMPLIANCE

Statement of Compliance
This Climate Report is prepared for the Co-operative Bank  
Limited (The Co-operative Bank) and its subsidiaries (together  
The Co-operative) and has been prepared in accordance with 
the Aotearoa New Zealand Climate Standards (NZCS) issued  
by the External Reporting Board (XRB). This Climate Report  
complies with those standards in all material respects.
This Climate Report is for the 
period 1 April 2023 to 31 March 
2024 which is the same as the 
financial reporting period for  
The Co-operative.
As this is The Co-operative’s initial 
Climate Report, there are a number 
of disclosure exemptions provided 
by NZCS which have been applied 
by The Co-operative in compiling 
this report.
The adoption provisions from NZCS2 
applied in preparing this report 
include exemptions from disclosing:
• Current financial impacts of
physical and transition impacts
• Anticipated financial impacts
of climate-related risks and
opportunities
• Transition planning aspects
of The Co-operative’s strategy
• Comparatives for Scope 3
GHG emissions
• Comparatives for metrics
• Analysis of trends in
reported metrics.
Disclaimer
This Climate Report contains climate-related and other forward-looking 
statements and metrics, which are not and should not be considered, 
guarantees, predictions or forecasts of future climate-related outcomes  
or financial performance. 
These statements are subject to known and unknown risks, uncertainties  
and other factors, which are beyond The Co-operative’s control. Readers  
are cautioned not to place undue reliance on such statements in light of  
the significant uncertainty in climate metrics and modelling that limit the 
extent to which they are useful for decision-making, and the many underlying 
risks and assumptions inherent in climate metrics and modelling may cause 
these statements to differ materially from actual future outcomes. 
This report has been produced for our existing and potential transacting 
shareholders however information in this Climate Report is not intended to 
be relied upon as advice to transacting shareholders or potential transacting 
shareholders and does not take into account the objectives, financial situation 
or needs of any particular transacting shareholder. A potential or existing 
transacting shareholder should consider their own legal, tax, and financial 
advisors in connection with any investment decision.
While we have prepared the information in this Climate Report based on 
our current knowledge, intentions and in good faith, we reserve the right to 
change our view in the future. 
For detailed information on our financial performance, please refer to  
The Co-operative Bank Disclosure Statements and Annual Report available 
on the website. 
This Climate Report was approved for issue by The Co-operative Bank Board 
on 3 June 2024.

Governance
This section provides relevant information to understand 
the Co-operative’s Board oversight of climate-related risks 
and opportunities, and the role that management plays in 
assessing and managing them.
Governance

is shown to the right.

The Co-operative Bank is the 
governance body responsible

GOVERNANCE
6
Board competency matrices 
include the requirement for the 
Boards to have knowledge and 
experience of climate-related 
risks and opportunities and their 
impact. Information and training 
will continue to be provided to 
directors to support their climate 
risk management oversight and 
implementation of climate reporting. 
All directors are members of their 
Board Risk Committee allowing a 
strong focus on climate risk matters 
by the Boards.
The Enterprise Risk Management 
Framework (ERMF) is fully 
implemented by management 
throughout The Co-operative by 
the Chief Risk Officer (CRO), a 
direct report of the Chief Executive. 
Reporting defined in the ERMF 
is provided by the CRO to the 
Boards and Risk Committees at 
every meeting, including detailed 
reporting and periodic deep dives 
into key risks. Climate-related risk is 
considered within the ERMF and  
the categorisation of “credit risk 
arising from climate change” as  
a “Key Risk” ensures this specific 
risk is considered at each Board 
meeting. Regular Key Risk reporting 
to the Boards and Risk Committees 
also includes consideration of 
emerging risks, and progress 
made by management in 
mitigating Key Risks.
In addition to ongoing risk 
management requiring action in 
the short and medium term through 
the ERMF, the Boards consider 
climate risks and opportunities as 
having the potential to impact our 
long-term strategic goals, and 
will give additional consideration 
to these matters at six-monthly 
strategic plan updates.
Management responsibility  
for climate-related risks  
and opportunities
The Board has delegated 
responsibility for execution of plans 
to mitigate identified climate risks 
to the Chief Executive. In turn the 
Chief Executive may delegate 
responsibility for execution of 
specific plans to the Senior 
Leadership Team (SLT).
The Chief Executive is responsible 
for ensuring appropriate training 
activities have been undertaken 
across the organisation while 
The Co-operative is developing 
the capability and skills required 
to identify, assess and manage 
climate-related risks and 
opportunities. This includes 
holding relevant workshops at 
the appropriate levels and use of 
experts as needed in the various 
workstreams of climate risk 
management and reporting.
The Chief Executive is responsible 
for ensuring plans are executed 
and targets that have been 
agreed with the Board are 
monitored, continuously assessed, 
and ultimately met. This includes, 
among other things, assessing  
how evolving risks impact The  
Co-operative’s operations, plans 
and strategy.
Results of these activities (including 
appropriate recommendations 
around developing or calibrating 
plans) are regularly reported to 
the Board and relevant Board 
Committees.
The SLT Risk and Operations Forum 
meets monthly and (among other 
risk-related activities) will regularly 
consider climate-related risks 
and opportunities and supports 
recommendations from the Chief 
Executive to the Board and direction 
to the business for responding to 
climate-related matters.
The Chief Risk Officer is tasked 
to lead activities around 
identification, assessment and 
integration of risks in various 
aspects of The Co-operative’s 
operations, including climate-
related risks and opportunities. 
This includes assessing credit 
exposure, incorporating climate 
risks into our risk management 
framework, and monitoring 
associated management activities 
where these risks arise.
The Chief Financial Officer 
manages the CRD reporting 
activities and plays a key role 
in ensuring that other climate- 
related activities (for example 
ESG, climate risk management, 
emissions targets and financial 
analyses) are efficiently interwoven 
to meet the reporting objectives  
of the Climate Standards. 
To support the Senior Leadership 
Team, tasks are assigned to 
various management levels 
within The Co-operative including 
Head of Group Strategy and 
Sustainability, Head of Credit, 
Head of Legal and Regulatory, 
Head of Risk and Compliance and 
Head of Financial Strategy.
Governance continued

These management positions 
report directly to the respective 
Senior Leadership Team members 
and are assigned specific roles in 
various climate-related activities 
of The Co-operative. Delivery 
and performance are monitored 
on a regular basis. These roles 
work in a collaborative manner 
and ensure that various climate- 
related activities are cohesively 
considered, efficiently executed 
and regularly reported to the 
Senior Leadership Team and 
Board committees.
No management remuneration  
is directly linked to climate- 
related risks and opportunities. 
Because the remuneration policy 
at our organisation does not 
support short-term incentives  
for specific targets, we do not  
have climate-related metrics  
and targets specifically noted 
in our remuneration policy.
We operate a profit share scheme 
that applies to all employees. 
As such, remuneration does not 
explicitly weight any climate-
related metrics or targets (or any 
other targets) towards a short 
term incentive.
Management remuneration 
is indirectly linked to climate-
related risks and opportunities to 
the extent that any SLT member, 
for example, the Chief Financial 
Officer or Chief Risk Officer, has 
a key performance objective 
to significantly progress our 
identification, assessment and 
management of climate risks and 
opportunities.

STRATEGY
8
Strategy
The Co-operative is a customer 
owned entity operating in retail 
banking and associated personal 
financial services across New Zealand.
With just over 400 staff, it provides 
financial products and services to 
over 180,000 customers including 
secured and unsecured loans, 
current accounts, other deposits and 
insurance. Products and services 
are provided remotely, through 
mobile apps, web applications 
and the phone, and face to face 
with nationwide coverage from 
Whangārei to Invercargill.
Our Head Office is in Wellington. 
We have a growing residential 
mortgage portfolio, but no 
commercial financing interests 
as we are solely a retail bank. In 
addition to retail banking, The 
Co-operative also markets and 
distributes life insurance products 
underwritten by its wholly owned 
subsidiary company Co-operative 
Life. 
The operations of Co-operative 
Life’s insurance business are in 
practical terms embedded in the 
operations of the Bank.
The Co-operative has set a strategy 
and each year will review it and set a 
business plan that is consistent with it, 
which involves an outside-in review 
of external conditions and a forward-
looking plan with goals. Strategic 
performance management occurs 
quarterly which involves reviewing 
strategic goals and the performance 
of top priority programmes. This 
process provides an opportunity 
to discuss the direction and impact 
of evolving strategy execution 
risks including climate risk. Carbon 
emissions reduction now forms an 
organisational objective against 
which performance is measured, 
and the initial work undertaken to 
identify, measure and manage 
climate risks and opportunities was  
a FY24 top priority programme for 
The Co-operative.
The effects of climate change 
on The Co-operative’s business 
model and strategy
Please refer to The Co-operative 
Bank Limited Annual Report for 
a full description of our business 
model and strategy.
The Co-operative recognises that 
climate change may affect its 
ability to continue with its current 
business model and execute its 
current strategy. This includes the 
potentially significant impact of 
climate change on our value chain, 
operations and financing decisions.
Our approach to considering 
climate change impacts as part 
of our strategy activity during the 
year involved various steps. We:
•	 Identified relevant climate- 
related risks and opportunities 
and an initial understanding of 
their corresponding impacts
•	 Performed exploratory scenario 
analysis to better capture and 
understand climate-related risks 
and opportunities for The Co-
operative, as well as to test the 
resilience of our business model 
and strategy
•	 Explored how climate change 
is contextualised in customers’ 
lives and in business operations 
in the future as we consider 
medium term operating model 
changes
•	 Set a science-aligned target*  
for GHG emissions reduction 
to manage our environmental 
impact
•	 Identified opportunities for  
The Co-operative to transition 
to a lower carbon emission 
economy over time
The Co-operative is committed to 
a balanced approach that takes 
into consideration environmental 
and social impacts along with 
economic development.
This involves implementing 
sustainable, socially-conscious  
and environmentally sound 
business practices, which have 
been verified externally as part  
of being a Certified B Corporation 
(B Corp). 
This way of working reflects our 
Purpose and Values expressed 
in our Core Foundations and 
supports an aspiration for  
long-term and sustainable 
outcomes for The Co-operative.
This section discusses how climate change currently impacts The Co-
operative and how it may do so in the future. Here we describe our  
scenario analysis undertaken, the risks and opportunities identified, and 
the development of The Co-operative’s plan to support a transition  
towards a low-emissions, climate-resilient future.
*  	 In respect of setting a science-aligned target, please refer to our discussion under Metrics and Targets section (page 23) of this report.

STRATEGY
9
Formulating the climate-related 
risks and opportunities into a 
holistic transition plan is a key step 
for the 2024/25 year and forms 
part of our strategic focus to build 
a stronger, scalable bank for the 
future. This includes considering 
the impacts of climate risks in 
relation to our capital deployment, 
financing and operational decisions 
as we develop and implement our 
transition plan and transition to 
a low-emissions, carbon-resilient 
future. 
Impacts of climate  
to The Co-operative 
Climate-related risks and 
opportunities are driven by 
transition and physical factors  
that have varying degrees of 
likelihood and impact to The  
Co-operative over time. Drivers 
of physical climate risks may 
include acute physical risks (such 
as increases in floods and storms) 
or chronic physical risks (such 
as drought or sea levels rising) 
while drivers of transition climate 
risks may include changes in 
government policy, technology, 
or market sentiment. In 
parallel, current and emerging 
opportunities exist in adopting 
climate resilient products, energy 
sources and implementing other 
efficiencies to build resilience as 
conditions continue to change.
To understand the practical 
impacts of a changing climate to 
our business, we have undertaken 
a process of risk identification and 
assessment of climate-related  
risks and opportunities.
Current impacts noted this year
Based on our assessment, we 
noted that the most material risk 
to our business relates to our 
residential mortgage lending 
portfolio where both physical 
and transition risks impact our 
customers’ ability to meet their 
financial obligations to us (credit 
risk). This will also be aggravated 
by direct and indirect impacts 
to our business operations (for 
example, our ability to attend 
to and support our customers 
through our network or the cost 
efficiency of running our day-
to-day operations in the face 
of potentially increasing costs 
due to climate transition risks) 
(operational risk).
We know from recent cyclone 
events in the North Island that 
assets that secure residential 
mortgage lending can be 
susceptible to climate risk. The 
actual physical damage caused 
to these properties, and questions 
over their future insurability can 
disrupt the ability of customers 
to service their debts in both 
the immediate aftermath of 
a severe weather event and for 
some time thereafter.  
While we have not sustained a loss 
in these recent events from a credit 
and asset valuation perspective 
(i.e. negative equity or under- 
insurance), we have noted how 
severe weather events may have 
both an immediate operational 
impact, and a flow-on effect to our 
financial position, performance, 
operation and current strategy.
Additionally, further developments 
in the regulatory space (for 
example, the implementation of 
the CRD regime) have required 
operational investment to meet 
current requirements, but we 
have also invested to enhance 
our current state so that we’re 
well-placed to respond to climate 
-related risk and opportunities 
going forward. This includes 
changes to how we measure our 
GHG emissions, set our targets 
and how we will develop and 
implement our transition plan to 
achieve progress against these 
targets in the future.
We detail in the following section the 
approach we applied; the key risks 
we have identified and assessed; 
and their corresponding potential 
impact to The Co-operative.
Strategy continued

10
Climate-related risks  
and opportunities for  
The Co-operative
Our approach involved a 
combination of relevant tools  
(e.g. scenario analysis) and 
methods noted in the Risk 
Management section of this 
report. Our scope included  
The Co-operative’s wider value 
chain (including our existing 
products, customers and 
operating channels) with a key 
focus for in-depth analysis (both 
qualitative and quantitative) 
concerning flood risks and macro 
economic risks to our residential 
mortgage lending portfolio.
Managing these risks and taking 
advantage of opportunities that 
may arise may require significant 
capital investment, and may 
include capital allocation to 
improve our response capabilities 
and potential changes to our 
lending decisions. This investment 
will be deployed to enhance 
our climate risk assessment 
and management capabilities 
(including training our people), 
improve our operational resilience 
to better support our customers 
and our people, explore new 
products that may incentivise 
decarbonisation, and in achieving 
our own GHG emissions targets.
As our journey takes a multi- 
year view, we used the following 
climate time horizons for our risk 
identification and assessment 
activities. We consider these 
horizons appropriate within the 
context of our business as a whole 
and, in particular, our residential 
mortgage lending portfolio which 
represents our most significant 
business exposure. These time 
horizons align with what has been 
adopted in the banking sector’s 
scenario analysis (see below) 
which allows for some degree of 
comparability across the industry.

The Co-operative’s current 
business planning horizons are  
as follows:
•	 Short term (1 year)

As we mature our climate 
adaptation response, we are 
considering the transitional and 
physical climate impacts on 
high-risk areas where we have 
concentrated lending, which 
affects our short-term business 
planning, capital allocation and 
financing decisions. 
This informs our business planning 
and required investments today. 
This will involve, for example, how 
we prioritise our existing resources 
in delivering our current strategic 
targets to also include investments 
in supporting our customers that 
may be affected by physical 
events, improving our climate 
risk management capabilities 
(particularly in respect of our 
lending portfolio), formulating 
action plans to respond to those, 
assessing how these risks impact 
our strategic lending growth 
targets, and achieving our GHG 
emission targets. 
The risks and opportunities form 
insight, data and assumptions 
that can be incorporated into our 
business and operating model, 
so that we can not only respond 
to manage the risk but our 
business and operating model is 
designed for it; this will include a 
consideration of our life insurance 
business in terms of risks and 
opportunities that may arise due  
to climate change.
In developing our Transition Plan, 
therefore, we will consider how 
our capital investments relating 
to our climate change response 
will be deployed over those 
climate time horizons and how 
these are incorporated into our 
regular business planning cycles. 
This will include how we consider 
the impact of climate change to 
our customers and our ability to 
support them as they go through 
their transition journey.
We summarise on the following 
pages the key climate-related risks 
and opportunities and how these 
may arise.

The risk that our customers’ homes

risk drivers
A reduction in insurance coverage on secured assets through physical damage, 
unaffordable cost of insurance, changes to insurance cover or insurance retreat, 
would result in increased levels of customer defaults, potential financial losses 
arising from non-recoverable loans balances, as well as significant disruption in 
our lending growth strategy. This would be exacerbated by an increased incidence 
of severe weather events due to a warming climate resulting in physical damage  
to property. The risk is increased in areas where The Co-operative has higher 
concentration of lending.
Credit risk
The risk that The Co-operative’s credit 
losses increase as our customers’ debt 
servicing capacity declines due to 
climate-related factors; this may result 
from items such as elevated energy 
prices, carbon taxation and the costs of 
mitigating physical risks or improving 
the energy performance of homes.
There is also the risk that credit losses 
are increased by loss of employment 
for borrowers as a result of physical 
risks or transition risks adversely 
impacting employers’ businesses.
Combination  
of physical  
and transition  
risk drivers
Adverse changes to borrower’s loan servicing capacity and/or employment status 
would result in increased levels of customer default, potential financial losses 
arising from non-recoverable loan balances, as well as significant disruption to our 
lending growth strategy. 
Adverse weather events causing flooding and/or other physical damage and 
interruptions in areas where we have higher concentration in our lending portfolio 
would result in non-recoverable lending balances, having a flow-on effect on 
our financial position, performance and cash flows. From a medium to long-
term perspective, this will have negative implications for our growth strategy and 
challenge the diversity of our lending portfolio as changes due to climate occur.
Capital and  
financial risk
The risk of market value loss, asset 
and liability management disruptions 
and access to capital due to climate 
change. This includes the risk that our 
capital buffer is insufficient to cover 
elevated credit losses in addition to 
increased operating costs as The 
Co-operative is exposed to increased 
occurrences of physical and transition 
risk events.
Combination  
of physical  
and transition 
 risk drivers
With increased risk of loss due to physical and transition impacts, we anticipate that 
our approach to capital deployment, prioritisation of funding and delivery of our 
current strategy will have to change. Increased credit losses and required spending 
to respond to climate change would result in reduction in our cashflows, disrupting 
achievement of our financial and growth targets.

Key risk category
Description
Type
How we anticipate this will impacts us
Operational risk
The risk that The Co-operative’s 
operating model, infrastructure, 
processes and systems may be 
disrupted due to increased physical 
risks (e.g. higher frequency of extreme 
weather events), rapid changes to 
climate-related regulations and 
market changes.
This area also includes opportunities 
associated with reducing the carbon 
emissions footprint of The Co-
operative, through policy, practice, 
behavioural and investment choices.
Combination  
of physical  
and transition  
risk drivers
Our current operating model will have to consider increased requirements to provide 
operational support to our customers and staff as changes due to climate impact the 
way we deliver our services from an infrastructure, value chain and delivery model 
perspective. We also recognise that as the economy transitions to a low emissions 
climate resilient model over time, the costs associated with this will have a flow-
on effect to our supply chain and our access to goods and services. Our internal 
processes and procedures will also need calibration as we navigate our way through 
the transition period (including changes in the regulatory and market areas).
In terms of the opportunity to reduce our operational carbon emissions, this could 
result in decreased costs to The Co-operative and increased customer loyalty among 
the segments of the market that The Co-operative chooses to target; development 
of capability, skillsets and access to technology will be required to support the 
transition, and allocation of capital deployment and funding will be influenced where 
these goals sit alongside others. Integration of carbon reduction to strategy is key to 
manage balanced investment decisions.
Conduct-related risk
The risk that The Co-operative may 
fail to comply with existing and 
new climate focused regulation or 
policy alongside other regulatory 
requirements (e.g. Our CoFI-related 
obligations to our customers).
Mostly  
transition risk
Failure to comply may potentially lead to fines, penalties and reputational damage.
Furthermore, accelerated changes in regulatory requirements could disrupt our 
current business model, strategy and our priority deliverables as we re-allocate 
our limited resources to respond. Also, as a relatively smaller bank, we could see 
increased challenge to manage non-compliance risk as the speed of change is 
combined with limited resources (i.e. as climate capability becomes in demand, 
we anticipate a decreased talent pool of suitable resources available in the market 
which, in turn, impacts The Co-operative’s ability to access these capabilities in an 
affordable manner).
Reputational risk
The risk that The Co-operative may 
fail to effectively implement and/
or communicate its climate-related 
actions, commitments and targets 
which may cause reputational 
damage; this may also arise from the 
inadequacy of our consideration of 
the impact of climate change to our 
business and customers.
Mostly  
transition risk
Our reputation may be damaged if we fail to effectively consider the impact of 
climate to our customers, our regulatory obligations, and our business model, 
strategy and operations. This will have a consequential negative impact in the  
way we retain and grow our customer base and sustain our business. 
Strategy continued

We also noted other risks that 
relate to climate in addition to the 
above material items including (i) 
model risk (given the long-term 
nature of climate risk factors, 
there is a risk that the availability 
and quality of data used in our 
scenario modelling may not be 
accurate or adaptable) and (ii) 
business model risk (which relates 
to our effectiveness in ensuring we 
adapt our current strategy to the 
evolving nature of climate change).
We identified that The Co-operative 
may also be able to take up 
opportunities to support the transition 
to a lower carbon economy for New 
Zealand by offering sustainable 
finance products and insight, use 
of green investments (e.g. bonds or 
carbon removal technology), and 
leveraging new technologies to 
support the transition.
Changes in customer demand 
and preferences along with

Modelling methodologies
The modelling approach selected 
were Beta regression and 
Generalised Additive Models 
(GAM). GAMs are powerful 
statistical models that allow for the 
modelling of complex non-linear 
relationships between variables 
(which we often see in econometric 
relationships); its key advantages 
include flexibility, interpretability, 
robustness and automatic variable 
selection. Both the Beta coefficients 
and the GAM curves serve as 
“pre-trained” models, allowing 
predictions to be generated in 
Excel for various climate scenario 
economic paths. On this basis, this 
modelling approach was used.
In respect of our climate scenario 
physical risk assessment, we 
use geo-spatial matching of The 
Co-operative’s portfolio data to 
climate change using the baseline 
flood plain scenario files; flood 
risk analysis is then used to extract 
flood depths and depth damage 
curves which are the basis for 
measuring property risk from 
potential extreme weather events 
under different climate scenarios. 
Property outlines and property 
coordinates are used to define 
the physical structure to capture 
possible flood damage; these 
outlines are overlayed across 
scenario maps and flood depths 
are iteratively extracted per 
building outline. All flood values 
are then taken and defined over 
the period of time covered in 
the time horizon on an iterative 
basis to achieve a reasonable 
level of refined accuracy. GAM is 
employed to capture the location-
specific relationships between 
the two variables, allowing for 
generalisations across Co-op’s 
own portfolio.
Limitations
The data sources cited above are 
based on information at the time 
we performed our analyses. Any 
changes thereto subsequent to 
that point may not be reflected 
in our results and assessments. 
Additionally, climate forecasts 
include a degree of uncertainty 
when identifying variables and 
assessing them as part of our 
scenario analysis and broader 
risk management approach. 
The analyses we performed, 
therefore, are based on national 
and international assumptions 
and data-sets and overlaying 
these with our internal information 
and sectoral level scenario 
analysis. The underlying limitations 
to these data and modelling 
sources should, therefore, be 
noted when reading this Climate 
Report. Lastly, the speed in which 
climate-related impacts are 
evolving are unprecedented and 
little reliance can be placed on 
historical experience to assess 
both magnitude and patterns. 
This gives rise to a higher level 
of uncertainty for banks when 
assessing the magnitude and 
timing of climate risk drivers. These 
drivers are also subject to tipping 
points that exacerbate uncertainty, 
particularly given geographic 
diversity of physical and transition 
impacts across New Zealand and 
the rest of the world.
